name: A. Lange & Söhne
tagline: Saxon haute horlogerie reborn in Glashütte after the fall of the Berlin Wall
summary: A. Lange & Söhne is Germany's most celebrated watchmaker, famous for its lavishly hand-finished German silver movements, outsize date and the Lange 1. Revived in 1990 and owned by Richemont since 2000, it is widely regarded as a peer of Patek Philippe in movement finishing.
history:
Ferdinand Adolph Lange, a Dresden-trained watchmaker, set up a workshop in the impoverished Saxon mining town of Glashütte in 1845 with government support, training local apprentices and effectively founding the German precision watch industry. His sons joined the business, and the firm became known for its pocket watches, the three-quarter plate and a distinctly Saxon approach to movement construction.

The company thrived into the 20th century, supplying pilots' observation watches during the Second World War. On the last day of the war in Europe, 8 May 1945, the main factory building was destroyed in a Soviet air raid. In 1948 the East German state expropriated the firm and folded it into the nationalised VEB Glashütter Uhrenbetriebe, and the Lange name disappeared for over four decades.

After German reunification, Walter Lange, great-grandson of the founder, teamed up with IWC and Jaeger-LeCoultre chief Günter Blümlein to re-register Lange Uhren GmbH on 7 December 1990. The first new collection of four watches, including the Lange 1 with its off-centre dial and patented outsize date, was unveiled in October 1994 and instantly established the revived brand at the top tier.

The manufacture passed to Richemont in 2000 when the group bought Les Manufactures Horlogères from Mannesmann. Since then Lange has produced landmark pieces such as the Datograph, the digital-display Zeitwerk (2009) and, in 2019, its first sports watch, the Odysseus. Every movement is assembled twice and finished to exceptionally high standards, including hand-engraved balance cocks.

name: Glashütte Original
tagline: Heir to Glashütte's state watch factory, now the Swatch Group's German manufacture
summary: Glashütte Original is the direct descendant of East Germany's nationalised watch combine GUB, privatised in 1994 and owned by the Swatch Group since 2000. It makes nearly everything in-house in Glashütte and is best known for its asymmetric Pano dials and Panorama Date big-date complication.
history:
Glashütte Original traces its roots to the Saxon watchmaking tradition that began in Glashütte in 1845. After the Second World War, the town's surviving firms, including Lange, were expropriated and in 1951 merged into the state-owned VEB Glashütter Uhrenbetriebe (GUB), which produced mass-market mechanical and later quartz watches for the Eastern Bloc for four decades.

With German reunification, GUB was converted into a limited company in 1990 and, in 1994, sold by the Treuhand privatisation agency to entrepreneur Heinz W. Pfeifer. The business was relaunched under the name Glashütte Original and repositioned as a maker of high-end mechanical watches, reviving historic calibres and developing new ones.

In 2000 the Swatch Group acquired the company, providing capital for a major expansion. Glashütte Original now produces its movements, dials (in its Pforzheim dial factory) and most components itself. Its signature designs include the PanoMatic family with its off-centre, asymmetrical dial layout, the Senator line of classic dress watches, and the retro-styled Sixties and Seventies collections.

The brand also supports local heritage: the Nicolas G. Hayek foundation established the German Watch Museum Glashütte in the company's former watchmaking school building in 2008. Glashütte Original continues to expand its line-up with dive watches such as the SeaQ and high complications including tourbillons and perpetual calendars.

name: Nomos Glashütte
tagline: Bauhaus-minimal watches with in-house movements at accessible prices
summary: Nomos Glashütte is an independent manufacture founded in 1990, just weeks after the Berlin Wall fell. Its clean, Bauhaus-influenced designs such as the Tangente, combined with in-house calibres and its own Swing System escapement, have made it one of the best-value German watchmakers.
history:
Nomos was founded in Glashütte on 1 January 1990 by Roland Schwertner, a Düsseldorf photographer and IT entrepreneur, taking its name from an earlier Glashütte firm that had briefly traded as Nomos in the early 20th century. The first four models, including the Tangente, appeared in 1992; their slim cases and restrained dials drew on 1930s German design and the functionalist ideals of the Deutscher Werkbund and Bauhaus.

Early Nomos watches used modified Peseux/ETA manual-wind movements, but the company steadily increased its manufacturing depth. It introduced its first self-winding in-house calibre in 2005 and, in 2014, unveiled the Nomos Swing System, its own escapement assembly including balance, hairspring and lever. This made Nomos one of very few independent brands able to produce its own regulating organ.

The ultra-thin DUW 3001 automatic calibre followed in 2015, powering the neomatik line. Nomos remains privately owned and headquartered in Glashütte, with a design studio in Berlin, and it has expanded its range with colourful Club, Tetra and Metro variants, world-timers and limited editions supporting charities such as Doctors Without Borders.

Known for honest pricing and thoughtful design, Nomos is frequently recommended as the entry point into Glashütte watchmaking and has won numerous design awards, including multiple iF and Red Dot prizes.

name: Moritz Grossmann
tagline: A 19th-century Glashütte master's name revived for exquisite hand-finished watches
summary: Moritz Grossmann is a small Glashütte manufacture founded in 2008 by watchmaker Christine Hutter, reviving the name of 19th-century horologist Carl Moritz Grossmann. It produces only a few hundred highly finished watches a year, noted for hand-annealed brown-violet hands and traditional Saxon movement architecture.
history:
Carl Moritz Grossmann (1826–1885) was one of the founding figures of Glashütte watchmaking. Born in Dresden, he trained in Switzerland, England and France before opening his own workshop in Glashütte in 1854 at the encouragement of his friend Ferdinand Adolph Lange. He won prizes for his writing on escapements, was elected to the Saxon parliament and initiated the German School of Watchmaking in Glashütte in 1878. After his sudden death in 1885 his business was wound up.

More than a century later, Christine Hutter, a trained watchmaker who had worked for Wempe, Maurice Lacroix, Glashütte Original and A. Lange & Söhne, acquired the rights to the dormant name and founded Grossmann Uhren GmbH on 11 November 2008, at the height of the financial crisis.

The first watch, the Benu, launched in 2010, followed by a purpose-built manufacture in Glashütte completed in 2013. The brand quickly earned critical acclaim for movements with untreated German silver plates, pillar construction and a manually operated stop-seconds mechanism, and for signature hand-crafted hands annealed to a brown-violet colour.

Moritz Grossmann has since expanded with the Tefnut, Atum and Hamatic lines and several tourbillons, including the Benu Tourbillon, notable for using a human hair in its stop-seconds brake. Production remains tiny, at roughly 200 watches a year, making it one of the most exclusive Glashütte houses.

name: Sinn
tagline: Frankfurt's engineering-led tool watches, tested for pilots, divers and astronauts
summary: Sinn Spezialuhren is a Frankfurt-based maker of instrument watches famous for proprietary technologies such as Tegiment hardening, Ar-Dehumidifying Technology and submarine-steel cases. Its pilot, diving and mission-timer watches are prized for robustness and value.
history:
Helmut Sinn, a former pilot and flight instructor, founded Sinn Spezialuhren in Frankfurt am Main in 1961. The company initially specialised in pilot's chronographs and cockpit clocks, selling directly to customers to keep prices down. Its watches earned credibility with professional aviators and, in 1985, German astronaut Reinhard Furrer wore a Sinn 140 S on the Spacelab D1 mission, making it the first automatic chronograph used in space.

In 1994 Helmut Sinn sold the business to engineer Lothar Schmidt, who had previously worked at IWC. Schmidt transformed Sinn into a technology-driven company, introducing innovations like the lubricant-free DIAPAL escapement, oil-filled HYDRO technology, Ar-Dehumidifying Technology to keep dials fog-free, and Tegiment surface hardening for scratch-resistant cases and bezels. The U1, launched in 2005, was the first watch made from German submarine steel.

Sinn continues to produce mission timers for German police special units (the EZM series) and has its watches independently tested and certified, including to the DIN 8330 pilot watch standard and by DNV for dive watches. Helmut Sinn died in 2018 at the age of 101. The company remains independent and family-run by the Schmidt family, with its own case manufacture, SUG, in Glashütte.

name: Junghans
tagline: Black Forest maker of the Max Bill icon and the first radio-controlled wristwatch
summary: Junghans, founded in Schramberg in 1861, was once the world's largest clock manufacturer. Today it is best known for the Bauhaus-inspired max bill watches and a pioneering role in radio-controlled and solar timekeeping.
history:
Erhard Junghans and his brother-in-law Jakob Zeller-Tobler founded the company in Schramberg in the Black Forest in 1861, initially making clock components before producing complete clocks. Adopting American-style industrial production methods, Junghans grew rapidly and by around 1903 was the largest clock factory in the world, employing some 3,000 people.

Wristwatch production began in earnest in the 1930s, and after the Second World War Junghans became one of Germany's biggest producers of chronometers. In 1956 the Diehl group took control of the company. Swiss architect and Bauhaus alumnus Max Bill designed a kitchen clock for Junghans in 1956 and a range of wristwatches in the early 1960s, whose minimalist dials remain the brand's best-known design.

Junghans was official timekeeper of the 1972 Munich Olympics and led the development of radio-controlled timekeeping: it launched radio-controlled table clocks in 1985 and, in 1990, the MEGA 1, the world's first radio-controlled wristwatch, followed by a solar-powered radio-controlled watch in 1993.

The company was sold to EganaGoldpfeil in 2000, but the new owner's collapse pushed Junghans into insolvency in 2008. In 2009 the Schramberg entrepreneur Hans-Jochem Steim and his son Hannes Steim acquired it, refocusing Junghans on design-led mechanical and quartz watches such as max bill, Meister and Form.

name: Stowa
tagline: Original wartime Flieger maker turned direct-to-consumer Bauhaus and pilot specialist
summary: Stowa, founded by Walter Storz in 1927, was one of the five original makers of the German B-Uhr pilot's watch. Revived by Jörg Schauer in 1996, it sells classic Flieger, Antea and Marine watches directly online at honest prices.
history:
Walter Storz founded Stowa (from STOrz WAlter) in 1927 in Hornberg in the Black Forest and moved the business to Pforzheim, Germany's watchmaking and jewellery centre, in 1935. In the 1930s Stowa produced the Antea, a clean Bauhaus-influenced design, and during the Second World War it was one of five companies contracted to build the large Beobachtungsuhr (B-Uhr) observation watches for Luftwaffe navigators, alongside A. Lange & Söhne, Laco, Wempe and IWC.

The Pforzheim factory was destroyed in an air raid in February 1945. Storz rebuilt, and in the post-war decades Stowa made a wide range of watches including the Seatime divers of the 1960s. Walter Storz's son Werner took over, but like much of the German industry the company struggled through the quartz era.

In 1996 Jörg Schauer, a Pforzheim-area watchmaker known for his own robust watches, acquired Stowa. He rebuilt the brand around faithful reinterpretations of its historic designs and became one of the first watch companies to sell primarily online direct to customers, keeping prices low. Stowa is now based in Engelsbrand near Pforzheim, where it assembles watches with Swiss movements and offers the Flieger, Antea, Marine, Partitio and Seatime lines.

name: Laco
tagline: Pforzheim pilot-watch specialist and one of the original B-Uhr makers
summary: Laco was founded in Pforzheim in 1925 and was one of the five firms that built Luftwaffe B-Uhr observation watches in the 1940s. Today it offers affordable to mid-priced Flieger watches, from Miyota-powered basics to faithful 'Original' reconstructions.
history:
Frieda Lacher and Ludwig Hummel founded Lacher & Co. in Pforzheim in 1925, producing watch cases and complete watches. Hummel went on to found the movement maker Durowe (Deutsche Uhren-Rohwerke) in 1933, while Erich Lacher, Frieda's son, ran the Erich Lacher Uhrenfabrik. The companies grew to about 1,400 employees by the mid-1950s.

During the Second World War, Laco was one of five manufacturers of the Beobachtungsuhr (B-Uhr), the oversized observation watch used by Luftwaffe navigators, alongside A. Lange & Söhne, Stowa, Wempe and IWC. These 55 mm watches established the Type A and Type B dial layouts that define pilot's watches to this day.

In 1959 Laco-Durowe was sold to the US company Timex, and in 1965 it passed to the Swiss Ebauches SA. The Erich Lacher Uhrenfabrik continued as a smaller company, and in 1988 Horst Günther acquired the Laco name and logo, allowing modern Laco watches to be produced again.

The company filed for insolvency in 2009 but restarted in 2010 under new management with a small team. Laco has since focused on pilot's watches, from entry-level automatic Flieger models to aged 'Erbstück' pieces and DIN 8330-certified watches, alongside navy and squad lines, all assembled in Pforzheim.

name: Mühle-Glashütte
tagline: Nautical instrument makers since 1869, building robust watches for rescuers and sailors
summary: Mühle-Glashütte is a family-run Glashütte company descended from Robert Mühle's 1869 precision-instrument workshop. Re-established in 1994, it makes marine chronometers and robust tool watches such as the S.A.R. Rescue-Timer, developed with the German Maritime Search and Rescue Service.
history:
Robert Mühle founded a precision-mechanics workshop in Glashütte on 22 April 1869, making measuring instruments for the town's growing watch industry. His sons joined the business, renamed R. Mühle & Sohn in 1905, and from 1918 it expanded into speedometers and car clocks.

After the Second World War the company was dismantled and absorbed into state enterprises. Hans Mühle re-established a small firm in December 1945, but in 1972 it too was expropriated and became part of the state-owned VEB Feinmechanik Glashütte. After reunification, Hans-Jürgen Mühle steered the business through privatisation and in 1994 re-founded the family company as Mühle-Glashütte GmbH nautische Instrumente und Feinmechanik, initially making marine chronometers, ship's clocks and nautical instruments.

The first Mühle wristwatches, a sports diver and the Marinefliegeruhr-I, went on sale in 1996. In 2002 the company delivered its first S.A.R. Rescue-Timers to the German Maritime Search and Rescue Service (DGzRS), and in 2003 it introduced its woodpecker neck regulation, a development of the swan-neck fine adjustment designed to keep the rate stable under shocks. Thilo Mühle took sole charge in 2007, and in 2011 the company presented the MU 9411, its first fully self-designed movement.

Today the family business, with the next generation joining management in 2024, offers robust tool watches for rescuers and sailors alongside accessible 29er sports watches and the classical Teutonia line.

name: Damasko
tagline: Bavarian materials specialists making ice-hardened, near-indestructible tool watches
summary: Damasko is a small manufacture in Barbing near Regensburg, founded in 1994 by materials engineer Konrad Damasko. It is known for ice-hardened steel and submarine-steel cases, patented crown seals and silicon hairsprings, and increasingly in-house movements.
history:
Konrad Damasko founded the company in 1994, applying high-performance materials technology he had developed for industries including aerospace. Its first major business was supplying hardened watch cases to Frankfurt's Sinn, a partnership that lasted until 2002, after which Damasko concentrated on watches under its own name.

The company built its reputation on metallurgy and engineering: ice-hardened stainless steel cases and bracelets, German submarine steel, its own DAMEST coating, patented crown and pusher sealing systems, and a patented silicon hairspring that resists magnetism and temperature changes. Damasko claims more than 100 patents, designs and utility models and says it produces demonstrably only in Germany, with manufacturing depth of up to 90 percent.

Around 2010 Damasko introduced its first in-house movement, the A35, followed by further automatic calibres and the C51 chronograph movement. Test pilots at Airbus Defence & Space have worn its DC-series chronographs. Still a family business with a team of around two dozen people, working from Barbing near Regensburg, Damasko sells through dealers and directly online, offering field watches (DK), divers (DSub), and pilot chronographs (DC) with a distinctly utilitarian aesthetic. Its utilitarian designs and genuine technical substance have earned the brand a loyal following among tool-watch enthusiasts worldwide.

name: Tutima
tagline: Glashütte pilot-chronograph pioneer that returned home after six decades in the West
summary: Tutima traces its roots to UROFA and UFAG, founded in Glashütte in 1927, whose 1941 Flieger chronograph became a German aviation icon. After decades in Ganderkesee near Bremen, the family-owned brand returned to Glashütte in 2011 and now makes in-house calibres including a minute repeater.
history:
In 1927, amid economic crisis in Glashütte, two companies were founded under the chairmanship of Dr. Ernst Kurtz: UROFA (Uhren-Rohwerke-Fabrik Glashütte AG), which made movements, and UFAG (Uhrenfabrik Glashütte AG), which made finished watches. Their best-quality watches carried the name Tutima, from the Latin 'tutus' for safe or secure. In 1941 the company produced the Tutima Flieger chronograph with calibre 59, a robust flyback chronograph issued to German pilots and now a highly collectible piece.

At the end of the Second World War, Ernst Kurtz left Glashütte for West Germany, and the Tutima name continued in Lower Saxony. The brand was later carried on by Dieter Delecate, and Tutima became based in Ganderkesee near Bremen. In 1984 Tutima supplied the Military Chronograph (NATO Chronograph) to the German Air Force, cementing its reputation for tool watches.

In 2011 Tutima returned to Glashütte, opening a new manufacture and presenting the Hommage minute repeater, followed by the in-house manual-wind calibre 617 in the Patria line. The brand remains owned by the Delecate family and offers pilot's watches, the M2 professional line, the Saxon One sport chronographs and the Patria dress watches.

name: Union Glashütte
tagline: Johannes Dürrstein's 1893 Glashütte name, revived by the Swatch Group
summary: Union Glashütte was founded in 1893 by Johannes Dürrstein to make fine yet affordable watches. Revived in the 1990s and part of the Swatch Group since 2000, it offers Glashütte-made mechanical watches at a lower price point than its sister brand Glashütte Original.
history:
Johannes Dürrstein, whose family firm Dürrstein & Co. already operated in Glashütte, founded the Uhrenfabrik Union in 1893 with the aim of producing high-quality watches that remained affordable. Union became known for precise pocket watches, including complicated pieces, and exported widely before the First World War.

The upheavals of the 20th century, including the world wars and the post-1945 nationalisation of Glashütte's watch industry into the state-owned GUB combine, brought the Union name to a halt for decades.

After German reunification the name was revived in the 1990s alongside the privatised Glashütte Original, and in 2000 both brands became part of the Swatch Group. Union Glashütte was positioned as the group's more accessible Glashütte brand, using Swatch Group-based automatic and manual calibres finished and assembled in Glashütte, many now fitted with silicon balance springs and long power reserves.

Unlike Glashütte Original, which builds complex manufacture calibres, Union Glashütte concentrates on reliable, well-finished everyday watches at more accessible prices.

Today the collection includes the sporty Belisar, the 1960s-inspired Noramis, the Averin and Seris, and the 1893 Johannes Dürrstein Edition, whose enamel-look dials, blued hands and railway-track chapter rings recall historic Glashütte pocket watches.

name: Hanhart
tagline: Black Forest chronograph specialist famous for its red pusher and Bundeswehr 417
summary: Hanhart was founded in 1882 in Diessenhofen, Switzerland, and has made watches and stopwatches in Germany's Black Forest since 1902. It is renowned for its 1930s pilot chronographs and the 417 issued to the West German military, whose red pusher became the brand's trademark.
history:
Johann A. Hanhart opened a watch shop and workshop in Diessenhofen, Switzerland, in 1882. In 1902 the business moved to Schwenningen in Germany's Black Forest, and it later settled in Gütenbach, where it still manufactures today. Hanhart made its first stopwatch in 1924 and became one of Germany's leading makers of affordable mechanical stopwatches.

In 1938 Hanhart introduced the Calibre 40 single-button chronograph, followed in 1939 by the two-pusher Calibre 41 with flyback function. These robust pilot's chronographs, including the TachyTele, were supplied to German aviators and are now highly collectible. Their red pusher, originally a safety measure to stop pilots accidentally resetting the chronograph, became Hanhart's visual signature.

In 1954 Hanhart created the 417 and the stainless-steel 417 ES for the newly formed West German Bundeswehr. Steve McQueen owned a 417 ES and wore it in the 1962 film The War Lover, helping make the model an icon. Like much of the industry, Hanhart struggled through the quartz era and went through several ownership changes in the 2000s and 2010s.

Today, led by co-CEOs Felix Wallner and Simon Hall, Hanhart produces reissues of the 417 ES and 415 ES, Pioneer and Primus pilot's chronographs and dive watches, assembled in Gütenbach with in-house tool-making and parts manufacture.

name: Chronoswiss
tagline: Born in a Munich garage during the quartz crisis, famed for the Régulateur and guilloché
summary: Chronoswiss was founded in Munich in 1983 by master watchmaker Gerd-Rüdiger Lang to champion mechanical watchmaking during the quartz crisis. Known for regulator dials, onion crowns, fluted bezels and hand-guilloché dials, it is now based in Lucerne, Switzerland.
history:
Master watchmaker Gerd-Rüdiger Lang founded Chronoswiss in Munich in 1983, shortly after losing his job when Heuer's German operation collapsed. At the height of the quartz crisis, he started building mechanical wristwatches from a garage full of parts, reviving rare calibres and emphasising transparent case backs that showed off the movement.

The brand found its signature in 1987 with the Régulateur, the world's first serially produced wristwatch with a regulator-style dial separating hours, minutes and seconds. It also established the design codes that still define Chronoswiss: the onion crown, straight lugs, finely fluted coin-edge bezel and a multi-part case. Further firsts followed, including the Kairos automatic chronograph with decentralised hours and minutes (1991), the reversible Cabrio (1992), the Opus skeletonised automatic chronograph (1995) and the Delphis (1996), which combined digital jumping hours, retrograde minutes and analogue seconds.

In 2012 Lang sold the company to the Ebstein family, who moved its headquarters and atelier to Lucerne, Switzerland. Under the new owners Chronoswiss has emphasised colourful hand-guilloché dials, bold regulators and new manufacture calibres such as the C.6000 family, developed with La Joux-Perret and introduced in 2023.

name: Kudoke
tagline: Stefan Kudoke's hand-engraved independent watches from rural Saxony
summary: Kudoke is the independent atelier of master watchmaker Stefan Kudoke, known for hand-skeletonised and engraved art pieces and the HANDwerk line built on his in-house Kaliber 1. His KUDOKE 2 and KUDOKE 3 both won the GPHG Petite Aiguille prize.
history:
Stefan Kudoke trained under two experienced master watchmakers and finished his apprenticeship as Brandenburg's state champion, placing third in the national craft-youth competition. He then joined Glashütte Original, working in its atelier for complications and prototypes, and later serviced Breguet, Blancpain and Omega watches in New York. He earned his master watchmaker's certificate at just 22.

Combining this training with studies in economics and finance, Kudoke set out on his own to design and make watches under his name. His early KUNSTwerk pieces, based on hand-skeletonised and hand-engraved movements, established his reputation, with creations such as the octopus-themed KudOktopus and the literal 'Real Skeleton' with an engraved skull.

The HANDwerk collection began with Kaliber 1, his first in-house manual-wind movement, featuring a raised, hand-engraved balance cock with his infinity motif. The KUDOKE 2 added a hand-engraved rotating day/night sky disc for 24-hour indication and won the GPHG Petite Aiguille prize in 2019; the unconventional three-armed hour display of the KUDOKE 3 won the same prize in 2024 in salmon.

Kudoke works from a small workshop in Weifa in Saxony with a tiny team, making watches largely to individual customer specifications.

name: Bremont
tagline: Aviation-inspired British watchmaker known for the ejection-seat-tested MB
summary: Bremont was founded in 2002 by brothers Nick and Giles English with the aim of reviving mechanical watchmaking in Britain. Known for rugged pilot's watches such as the Martin-Baker MB series, it assembles and increasingly manufactures watches at its facility in Henley-on-Thames.
history:
Brothers Nick and Giles English grew up restoring vintage aircraft with their father. The name Bremont comes from a French farmer, Antoine Bremont, who sheltered them after they made an emergency landing in France in 1995. After their father died and Nick was badly injured in a 1996 plane crash, the brothers decided to pursue their dream of building mechanical watches in Britain, founding Bremont in 2002.

The brand quickly built an aviation identity. Its partnership with ejection-seat maker Martin-Baker produced the MB series, which is tested on live ejection rigs; the red-barrelled MBI is available only to those who have ejected from an aircraft using a Martin-Baker seat. Bremont also partnered with military units, explorers and motorsport teams, and developed Trip-Tick case construction and a rubber-mounted, shock-protected movement.

In 2021 the company opened The Wing, a manufacturing and technology centre in Henley-on-Thames, where it machines components and assembles watches, alongside its first in-house-designed calibre. In 2023 an investor group led by Bill Ackman took a major stake, and in 2024 Davide Cerrato was appointed CEO, launching a streamlined collection built around the Supermarine, Altitude, Terra Nova and Supernova families and a new logo.

name: Christopher Ward
tagline: English-designed, Swiss-made watches sold direct at honest prices
summary: Christopher Ward is a direct-to-consumer British brand founded in 2004 that designs in England and builds its watches in its own atelier in Biel, Switzerland. Famous for strong value, the C60 Trident diver and the GPHG-winning Bel Canto, it has become one of the best-known British watch brands.
history:
Christopher Ward was founded in 2004 by three friends with retail backgrounds: Mike France, Peter Ellis and Chris Ward. Their idea was simple: sell well-made Swiss watches directly online, cutting out the middlemen and pricing each watch at roughly three times its production cost rather than the much higher multiples typical of the industry.

The brand grew quickly through the late 2000s with dress watches, pilots and the C60 Trident dive watch, which became its best-seller. It built a close relationship with Swiss movement specialist Jörg Bader and watchmaker Johannes Jahnke, which led to Christopher Ward's own in-house calibre, the SH21 (later known as CW001), introduced in 2014 and billed as the first commercially viable mechanical movement from a British brand in over 50 years. Jahnke also created the JJ-series modules used for jumping hours and chiming complications.

All Christopher Ward watches are hand-built in its atelier in Biel, Switzerland, while design and the head office are in Maidenhead, England. In 2022 the brand launched The Twelve, its dodecagonal integrated-bracelet sports watch, and in 2023 the C1 Bel Canto, a chiming watch priced under $5,000, made Christopher Ward the first British brand to win a Petite Aiguille at the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève. The company commits 2 percent of sales to charitable causes.

name: Roger W. Smith
tagline: George Daniels' only apprentice, hand-making watches on the Isle of Man
summary: Roger W. Smith OBE is widely regarded as the world's finest living watchmaker, the protégé of George Daniels. His small Isle of Man workshop makes around 15–20 watches a year entirely by hand using the Daniels Method, each built around a co-axial escapement.
history:
Roger Smith enrolled at the Manchester School of Horology at 16 in 1986, winning the British Horological Institute's Bronze Medal as its top student. After hearing George Daniels lecture, he resolved to make a watch entirely by hand, and completed his first pocket watch, with a one-minute tourbillon and detent escapement, at 22. Daniels rejected it as not good enough; Smith's second pocket watch, adding a perpetual calendar, won Daniels' approval.

Daniels then invited Smith to the Isle of Man to help create the Daniels Millennium series of co-axial wristwatches, making him Daniels' only apprentice. Smith subsequently founded Roger W. Smith Ltd in a converted bedroom in Ballaugh, Isle of Man, beginning with a series of unique tourbillon wristwatches.

In 2004 he began designing the Series 2, finishing the prototype in 2006; it was the first production movement designed specifically around the Daniels co-axial escapement. Over the following years he refined the co-axial into his own single-wheel version. Later came the Series 1, 3, 4 (whose first piece, delivered in 2020, was the 100th watch made under his name), 5 and 6.

Smith was awarded an OBE in 2018 for services to British watchmaking and continues to lead a small team making almost every component in-house, producing around 15 to 20 watches a year with waiting lists of several years.

name: Fears
tagline: Bristol watchmaker from 1846, revived by the founder's great-great-grandson
summary: Fears was founded in Bristol in 1846 by Edwin Fear and made watches for 130 years before closing in 1976. Revived in 2016 by Nicholas Bowman-Scargill, it is known for the curvaceous cushion-cased Brunswick and small-batch watches hand-built in Britain.
history:
Edwin Fear founded the company in Bristol in 1846, on Redcliff Street, and it grew into a respected watch and jewellery business supplying pocket and then wrist watches under the Fears name. By the 1920s and 1930s the company was producing elegant cushion and rectangular wristwatches, several of which inspire today's designs, including a 1924 gentleman's cushion-case watch and a 1930 art deco rectangular piece.

Like much of the British watch trade, Fears was hit by changing markets in the post-war decades, and the business closed in 1976.

In 2016 Nicholas Bowman-Scargill, the great-great-grandson of Edwin Fear, relaunched the brand in Bristol. The first new models were the modestly priced Redcliff, named after the street where the company was founded, followed by the Brunswick, whose cushion case has no flat surfaces and a signature onion crown. In 2021 the brand celebrated its 175th anniversary with the Archival 1930, a proportional recreation of a 1930 rectangular watch using original vintage movements.

Fears now hand-builds its watches in small batches in Bristol and has expanded with the Brunswick 38, 40 and 40.5 Jump Hour (the latter using a Christopher Ward JJ01 module) and the Redcliff 39.5 with La Joux-Perret movements, winning a following among collectors for its refined, understated style.

name: Garrick
tagline: Norwich workshop hand-making dials, hands and movement parts for British fine watches
summary: Garrick is a small British watchmaker founded by David Brailsford and Simon Michlmayr, based in Norwich, Norfolk. It makes dials, hands and many movement parts in-house, using rose engines for guilloché and producing watches in very small numbers to order.
history:
Garrick was founded by David Brailsford and Simon Michlmayr with the ambition of building genuinely British fine watches, shunning mass production in favour of limited numbers of hand-finished pieces. The company set up its own workshop in Norfolk, where dials, hands and a multitude of movement components are made in-house, and its guilloché dials are engine-turned on historic rose and straight-line engines.

In 2016 Garrick released the Portsmouth, its first watch with an exclusive movement, the Calibre UT-G01, developed with a Swiss movement specialist. Further calibres followed, including the UT-G02 used in the Regulator with its visible free-sprung 'Trinity' balance.

The brand has since moved further into high horology with the S2 Deadbeat Seconds, powered by the Calibre DB-G06, and the S3, whose MK2 version has an openworked dial and the UT-G04 calibre with screwed chatons and black polishing. The more accessible S7 uses a modified vintage manual movement with a fully customisable engine-turned dial.

Garrick works from a clean-room workshop with positive air pressure in Norwich, building every watch to order, and has become one of the leading names in the small revival of British watchmaking.

name: Baltic
tagline: Besançon microbrand making vintage-inspired watches at honest prices
summary: Baltic is a French microbrand founded by Etienne Malec in Besançon, selling vintage-inspired divers, chronographs and dress watches directly online. Its affordable micro-rotor MR01 and Aquascaphe diver made it one of the most successful microbrands of its generation.
history:
Etienne Malec founded Baltic in 2016, inspired by his father, a photographer and passionate collector who documented every watch he encountered in a diary. The name nods to the family's Polish roots and the Baltic Sea. Launched through crowdfunding, the brand's first model, the Bicompax 001 manual chronograph, quickly sold out and set the tone: 1950s and 1960s-inspired designs, faithful proportions and prices within reach of young enthusiasts.

Baltic followed with the HMS 001 dress watch and, in 2020, the Aquascaphe, a compact vintage-style diver that became its best-seller. In 2021 the MR01, a sub-€600 dress watch with a micro-rotor movement, a salmon dial and Breguet numerals, won widespread acclaim.

The company designs its watches in Besançon, the historic heart of French watchmaking, sourcing components from Hong Kong and elsewhere and assembling and adjusting watches in its Besançon atelier, with straps made in France. Sold primarily direct to consumers and through a small number of retailers and showrooms, Baltic has broadened its line-up with GMT divers, the Hermétique field watch, the Scalegraph chronograph with a Sellita manual chronograph movement and stone-dial Prismic models.

name: Yema
tagline: French tool-watch maker behind the Superman diver and the first French watch in space
summary: Yema was founded in Besançon in 1948 and became France's leading watch exporter, known for the 1963 Superman dive watch and the Rallygraf and Navygraf lines. Now based in Morteau, it has revived its heritage models and developed its own CMM micro-rotor and automatic calibres.
history:
Henry-Louis Belmont founded Yema in Besançon in 1948. The brand grew rapidly in the 1950s and 1960s with robust sports watches, becoming one of France's largest watch exporters. Its best-known model, the Superman dive watch of 1963, featured a patented bezel-lock system secured by the crown guard, and was adopted by divers and French military users. Yema also produced the Rallygraf chronograph for motorsport, the Navygraf diver and the Yachtingraf regatta timers.

In 1982 French astronaut Jean-Loup Chrétien wore a Yema Spationaute during the Soviet-French Soyuz T-6 mission, making it the first French watch in space. The same year the company was acquired by Matra, and in 1988 it was sold to Japan's Hattori Seiko group.

In 2009 Yema was bought by Montres Ambre, a family watch group based in Morteau on the French-Swiss border, which moved the brand there. Over the following decade Yema relaunched its heritage icons through successful crowdfunding campaigns and, from 2021, introduced its own movements developed under the Manufacture Morteau banner: the CMM.20 micro-rotor calibre, followed by the CMM.10 automatic, the CMM.29 slim micro-rotor and even a tourbillon. Today Yema offers everything from affordable meca-quartz Rallygrafs to chronometer-precision Supermans, with official partnerships including the French Navy.

name: Lip
tagline: France's oldest watch brand, known for presidents' watches and the Mach 2000
summary: Lip was founded in Besançon in 1867 by Emmanuel Lipmann and became France's most famous watchmaker, supplying watches to heads of state and pioneering electric timekeeping. Today it offers affordable heritage designs such as the Himalaya, Général de Gaulle and Roger Tallon's Mach 2000.
history:
Emmanuel Lipmann founded a small watchmaking workshop in Besançon in 1867, and the family business, later branded Lip, grew into the largest watch manufacturer in France. Its T18 calibre watches of the 1930s and 1940s became symbols of French precision; after the Liberation, Lip watches were presented to Winston Churchill and General de Gaulle, earning the Général de Gaulle model the nickname 'the watch of presidents'. Mountaineer Maurice Herzog's Annapurna expedition of 1950 is linked to the Himalaya model.

Under Fred Lip, the founder's grandson, the company pursued technical innovation, including early electric wristwatches developed in the 1950s. In the 1970s it commissioned avant-garde designs from industrial designer Roger Tallon, whose asymmetric Mach 2000 of 1975 is now considered a design classic.

Financial troubles led to the famous 'Lip affair' of 1973, when workers at the Palente factory in Besançon occupied the plant and continued to produce and sell watches themselves, becoming a landmark of French labour history. The company was eventually liquidated, and the brand passed through several owners in the following decades.

In the mid-2010s the Lip brand returned to Besançon under new owners, who revived its heritage models and developed the R26, described as the first automatic movement made in Besançon since the Fred Lip era, with most components sourced in France.

name: Raketa
tagline: Peter the Great's 1721 Peterhof factory, making watches named for Gagarin's flight
summary: Raketa is the watch brand of the Petrodvorets (Peterhof) Watch Factory near St Petersburg, founded as Peter the Great's imperial lapidary works in 1721. Named in honour of Gagarin's 1961 flight, it is one of the few factories that makes every part of its movements, including hairsprings.
history:
Peter the Great founded the Imperial Peterhof Factory in 1721 beside his summer palace outside St Petersburg to cut and carve hardstones for the new imperial capital. For two centuries it produced lavish stone objects as imperial gifts, and in Soviet times it made monumental works such as the Kremlin stars. In 1938 the factory began producing ruby jewels for watch movements.

After the Second World War, the factory launched the Pobeda watch in 1945 on the Kremlin's orders, and in 1961 the Raketa ('rocket') brand was created in honour of Yuri Gagarin's first human spaceflight. Raketa became one of the Soviet Union's largest watchmakers, developing the 24-hour Polar watch for the Soviet Antarctic Expedition in 1970, the famous Big Zero, and the official watches of the 1980 Moscow Olympics.

After a difficult period following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the factory began a modernisation programme in 2011 with new investors, reviving Soviet-era designs and investing in its own manufacturing. Raketa now produces every part of its mechanical movements in Peterhof, including the hairspring, and has introduced its own automatic calibre and playful designs such as the Copernicus and the counterclockwise Russian Code. In 2021 the factory celebrated its 300th anniversary.

name: Vostok
tagline: Chistopol's Soviet military watchmaker behind the Komandirskie and Amphibia
summary: Vostok is made by the Chistopol Watch Factory in Tatarstan, established in 1942 when a Moscow watch plant was evacuated during the Second World War. Its Komandirskie military watches and ingeniously sealed Amphibia divers are among the cheapest in-house mechanical watches in the world.
history:
In 1941–42, as German forces approached Moscow, the Second Moscow Watch Factory was evacuated to the small Volga town of Chistopol in Tatarstan. The relocated plant began producing watches and military instruments for the Red Army, and after the war it stayed in Chistopol, becoming the Chistopol Watch Factory, which adopted the Vostok ('East') brand name in the 1960s.

Vostok became a major supplier to the Soviet Ministry of Defence. In 1965 it introduced the Komandirskie ('commander's') watch for officers, and in 1967 the Amphibia, a dive watch rated to 200 m that uses a clever sealing design in which water pressure pushes the crystal and caseback more tightly against their gaskets. Its sturdy, simple in-house movements, including the 2409 manual and 2415/2416 automatics, earned a reputation for reliability.

After the collapse of the Soviet Union the factory was privatised and faced repeated financial difficulties, but it continued making its own movements and cases. Vostok watches became a cult favourite among Western enthusiasts thanks to their low prices, endless dial variants and ease of modification. In 2017 the factory marked the 50th anniversary of the Amphibia with a 1967-style reissue, and it continues to produce Amphibia, Komandirskie and special editions today.

name: Poljot
tagline: The First Moscow Watch Factory brand that timed Gagarin's flight and Leonov's spacewalk
summary: Poljot ('flight') was the brand of the First Moscow Watch Factory, founded in 1930, whose Sturmanskie was worn by Yuri Gagarin and whose Strela chronograph went on the first spacewalk. The Soviet-era factory has since closed; the name lives on through Poljot-International in Alzenau, Germany.
history:
The First State Watch Factory was established in Moscow in 1930, using machinery and tooling bought from the defunct Dueber-Hampden company in the United States, and was later named after Sergei Kirov. It produced the first mass-market Soviet watches and, after the war, pilot's watches such as the Sturmanskie ('navigator's'), a version of which Yuri Gagarin wore on the first human spaceflight in 1961. Following that flight, the factory's watches took the name Poljot, meaning 'flight'.

In 1959 the factory introduced the Strela chronograph with calibre 3017, issued to Soviet pilots and cosmonauts; Alexei Leonov wore one during the first spacewalk in 1965. From the 1970s the factory produced the calibre 3133 chronograph, based on the Swiss Valjoux 7734, which powered the Okeah naval chronograph and many export Poljot chronographs.

After the collapse of the Soviet Union the factory was privatised and struggled, and Poljot-branded movement production eventually ceased. In 1992 the distributor Poljot-V GmbH was founded in Frankfurt, and in 1994 the Poljot-International brand was created under Alexander Shorokhov. Now based in Alzenau, Germany, Poljot-International designs and assembles mechanical watches inspired by the Russian tradition, while the Sturmanskie and Strela names are used separately by other Russian companies.

name: Prim
tagline: Czechoslovakia's national watch, made in Nové Město nad Metují since 1949
summary: Prim is the Czech watch brand born in 1949 when the state enterprise Chronotechna set out to build Czechoslovakia's first wristwatches in Nové Město nad Metují. Millions of 'Primky' were made, and today the brand produces its own manufacture calibres alongside heritage models such as the Spartak and Orlík.
history:
On 6 November 1949, Adolf Martínek and fifteen colleagues set up a new branch of the national enterprise Chronotechna in an empty building in Nové Město nad Metují, tasked with making the first Czechoslovak wristwatches. Using calculations based on the French Lip R25 calibre, they produced twelve prototypes in 1954 under the name Spartak. Serial production began in 1957, and at the end of that year a ministerial commission decided the wristwatches would carry the Prim name, previously used for alarm and wall clocks. The first watches reached customers in 1958.

The 1960s brought the models that defined the brand, including the Pavouk, the Diplomat, the Sport and the Orlík, developed in 1965 for the Czechoslovak army. In 1969 the factory became independent from Chronotechna as Elton, and by the end of the 1980s around 15 million Prim watches had been made in Nové Město.

Privatisation after 1990 split the business: the Frýdek-Místek operation obtained the PRIM trademarks in 2001, starting a dispute over the brand that lasted more than twenty years. In June 2025 Petr Hanko, owner of MPM-Quality, bought Elton hodinářská from the CSG group, reuniting the brand, and in 2026 a unified logo based on the 1956 original was introduced. Prim now makes watches in both Nové Město nad Metují, home to its manufacture calibres, and Frýdek-Místek.
